parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: What are your main day-to-day responsibilities, and what workflows do you need this new service to handle for you?

As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights by deciding which drone flies along which way, and I sign off each flight before it leaves. My legal responsibility includes choosing the drone and the way it flies, and I am the licensed person who can call off a flight. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts.
ASK technician: What are your main day-to-day responsibilities, and what workflows do you need this new service to handle for you?

My responsibilities are keeping drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, and send drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back in service.
ASK desk: What are your main day-to-day responsibilities, and what workflows do you need this new service to handle for you?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
ASK desk: Who employs the airspace desk role, and what exact information can the airspace desk see or not see about customer companies' sites, drones, and flights?
I work for the platform company, not any of the customer companies. The airspace desk works for all customer companies and has no business looking into any one company's operations.
ASK desk: Since customer sites are private to each company, how are flight corridors between sites defined and managed without exposing customer sites to the desk or to other companies?
